A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GCD/AOL watermark-detection work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and relocation of material.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification, localization, text-length, and attack experiments using C4 and Arxiv texts, including numerical results in Tables 1–4.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds measured runtime and detection/localization results comparing WinMax, GCD, and AOL in Table 3.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain geometric-cover interval testing, FPR calibration, circular Aligator initialization, prediction averaging, and thresholding. The new comparisons and explanations do not establish a change to the proposed procedures.

E1.justification: Both versions use C4 and Arxiv for watermark classification and localization. The multiple-watermark scenario, varying text lengths, and swapping, deletion, and paraphrasing attacks are retained. The efficiency comparison introduces no reported new dataset or task scenario.

E2.justification: V2 adds an evaluated, directly relevant competing method: WinMax, in WinMax-1 and WinMax-100 configurations, with TPR, IoU, and runtime comparisons in Table 3. V1 only discussed WinMax in related work. The existing VANILLA and RoBERTa comparisons remain.

E3.justification: V2 adds average runtime per sample as an evaluation metric and tests WinMax configurations described as 1-token and 100-token windows. Existing dataset construction, sample counts, generation settings, baseline training, and FPR/IoU evaluation remain unchanged. Table 3 does not clearly identify its specific dataset/model/watermark and FPR setting.

E4.justification: V2 adds a GCD-only versus AOL localization ablation in Table 3, reporting IoU of 0.387 versus 0.718. It also states that other circular-start counts were explored, without presenting a numerical sweep. The boundary-artifact example, multiple-watermark test, length analysis, and attack experiments already appeared in v1.

E5.justification: The FPR calibration procedures and point-estimate reporting are retained. V2 introduces no experimental run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. AOL's circular random starts remain algorithmic iterations rather than repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: New Table 3 supplies the first measured efficiency/accuracy comparison: WinMax-1, WinMax-100, GCD, and AOL take 3643.61, 33.90, 1.24, and 2.18 seconds, respectively, all reporting TPR 0.99. Their IoUs are 0.980, 0.791, 0.387, and 0.718, exposing an important speed–localization tradeoff. All original numerical tables are unchanged: v1 Tables 3–4 become v2 Tables 4–5.

T1.justification: The segment-estimation bound changes its leading normalization from 1/(j-1) in v1 Section 3.3 to 1/(j-i) in v2 Section 3.2. This is a limited mathematical correction. The remaining estimation guarantees and appendix calibration mathematics are retained, with no new proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: efficient partial-watermark classification and localization using GCD and AOL, broad applicability, and strong empirical performance. The added efficiency evidence does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the measured WinMax computation/accuracy tradeoff and explicitly argues that 10 circular starts balance accuracy and cost. Appendix A.1 newly justifies the 10% watermark ratio as plausible and sufficiently detectable. The existing limitations paragraph is relocated to the main text without substantive change.

D1.justification: V2 adds a public-code repository link in the abstract and identifies the timing server's AMD EPYC 9354 processor and Nvidia A6000 GPUs in Appendix A.4. It also documents the WinMax configurations. Existing dataset-generation and RoBERTa-training details largely move to Appendix A.

R1.justification: V2 adds Dathathri et al. (2024) and a discussion of SynthID's use in Google Gemini, modestly extending the practical context. WinMax and its efficiency relationship to AOL were already discussed in v1; its new experimental participation is a baseline change.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: v1 Sections 4.1–4.4 move into Appendix A, while v2 supplies a condensed main-text settings subsection. Calibration becomes Appendix B, limitations move into the main paper, and the separate Problem Statement heading is absorbed into Section 3. Most underlying prose is retained.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document from single-column to two-column layout, substantially resizing and repositioning tables, algorithms, and figures. Figure 2 moves from the results discussion to the method pages, a runtime table is added, table rules are revised, and several captions are clarified. Existing plotted results remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The WinMax runtime comparison and GCD-only ablation strengthen empirical support for the efficiency and localization design. The code pointer, hardware disclosure, and mathematical correction also improve documentation. The gain remains limited because the new benchmark's precise setting is unclear, uncertainty is unreported, and its results show a speed–localization tradeoff, with AOL less accurate than WinMax by IoU.
